newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Feb 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Feb 26.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
- - - - DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- MIRROR REBUFFED OVER MIN SHARES

Brokers to the Mirror Group, SBC Warburg, have been rebuffed after approaching Schroder Investment Management, the largest institutional investor in Midland Independent Newspapers (MIN), to see if it would sell its stake. It is thought that SBC Warburg's initial offer was pitched too low because of the high multiples that regional newspaper groups were sold for last year. After the rebuff, SBC Warburg is believed to have let the matter drop.
-- MORGAN PROBES YOUNG ACCOUNT IN CAYMANS

Investigators at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell have uncovered an account in the Cayman Islands established by former fund manager Peter Young. The Cayman Islands-based account is called Russ Oil and Technology, and was set up several months before Young was dismissed. It is believed that Zurich-based lawyers Juerg Wyler and Marco Wolf aided Young with the documentation. However, it is not clear if the account was activated by Young before his unauthorised trading activities were discovered.
-- ELTON JOHN BIDS FOR LOTTERY CASH

Elton John's Rocket Pictures is to join with Merchant Ivory Productions to apply for 34 million sterling of lottery money to finance films over the next six years. Other members of the consortium include EMI Music Publishing, HTV, Yorkshire Tyne-Tees Television and various movie producers. Capital Films would add more than 50 million sterling to the money from the Arts Council and advance sales to America are forecast to generate another 36 million sterling.
THE TIMES
-- NATWEST HIT BY COST OF RESTRUCTURING

NatWest have reported huge restructuring costs and have given no indications of when it might begin a new programme of buying back shares. The bank also revealed that it had dropped out of the bidding for mutual life company Scottish Amicable. Chief executive Derek Wanless confirmed he had signed an agreement to inspect the mutual's finances, but had decided the price was too high. He also warned that it was becoming more cautious on lending to small businesses, property and construction companies.
-- SEVENTH BARINGS DIRECTOR BANNED BY SFA

James Bax has become the seventh former director of Barings to be banned by the Securities and Futures Authority after its inquiry into the merchant bank's collapse. He was in charge of the office where Nick Leeson worked. He accepted the ruling and is now banned for 21 months and has been ordered to pay 10,000 sterling expenses. He said he could not afford the costs of defending himself against the charges.
-- WIMPEY EXPECTING A PEAK YEAR

The UK's biggest house retailer, George Wimpey, have reported doubled pre-tax profits of 31.5 million sterling and said it expected 1997 to be a peak year for the housing market. Chairman Joe Dwyer said that Wimpey had enjoyed buoyant trading in the first eight weeks of this year and said that rising house prices are feeding through to the new homes market. He also expressed little concern about the effect of the forthcoming general election.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FLAT MUSIC FAILS TO SPICE UP EMI

EMI, the music company, has reported a 30 million sterling profit shortfall in the three months to the end of December. US sales had slumped by almost a third as the company's Virgin Music and Capitol labels felt the effects of a flat music market, made worse by a poor release schedule which lacked the hits of the same quarter in 1995. A strong sterling also helped to drive profits from the U.S. down from 47 million sterling to 18 million in the three-month period.
-- ATTACKS ON EU SOCIAL PLANS 'OVERBLOWN'

A report by the independent Employment Policy Institute suggests government claims that signing up to the European Social Chapter would cost half a million jobs is "overblown, inaccurate and unresearched". The institute argues that the Social Chapter would not impose massive costs on UK employers and could increase the adaptability of the workforce. John Philpott, the institute's director, said the Social Chapter could overcome the insecure "hire and fire" environment in the UK labour market.
-- CHRISTIAN SALVESEN ROW INTENSIFIES

Sir George Elliot, former chairman at Christian Salvesen, the distribution and equipment hire company, has urged investors to vote against the 150 million sterling special dividend it plans to pay later this year. He says he has support from investors controlling 14 per cent of Salvesen's shares and has written to shareholders outlining his objections to the plan, which he says will weaken the group's financial strength.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- UNION UP FOR SALE AS ERA OF DISCOUNT HOUSES REACHES END

Union, the City company which made its reputation as a discount house, is up for sale and there are expectations of substantial job losses. Joseph Lewis, the millionaire who owns Christie's auctioneers, could buy the company. A non-executive director, Graeme Knox, is to temporarily take over as chairman. He said the company had received several unsolicited bid approaches over the past few weeks and was pursuing discussions with the interested parties.
-- BZW SET TO APPEAL AGAINST BID RULING BY PANEL

Investment banking arm of Barclay's Bank, BZW, is considering appealing against a secret provisional ruling made by the Takeover Panel over its role in the hostile battle for control of Northern Electric. It is thought that the Panel executive, which is made up of City professionals on secondment from merchant banks and accountants, is proposing to criticise aspects of BZW's conduct as broker to Northern during its unsuccessful defence of the 782 million sterling bid from US power generator CalEnergy.
-- EMU 'BACKED BY BOND YIELDS'

Speaking at the Euromoney International Bond Congress in London, Eddie George, Governor of the Bank of England, said that bond dealers expect European monetary union to go ahead on time. He said that because yield curves in Germany and France are practically identical it is consistent with EMU going ahead. Leading commercial economists diverged from the bond market view, expressing doubts that EMU would go ahead on time.
